claim: Chromatin has been shown to undergo diffusional motion, which is affected during gene transcription by RNA polymerase activity.
source: Chromatin has been shown to undergo diffusional motion, which is affected during gene transcription by RNA polymerase activity.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that references established knowledge about chromatin motion and transcription.

claim: Chromatin motion was locally constrained at the sites of DNA replication.
source: By correlating chromatin mobility proximal to the active sites of DNA synthesis, we showed that chromatin motion was locally constrained at the sites of DNA replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: Inhibiting DNA synthesis led to increased loading of DNA polymerases.
source: Furthermore, inhibiting DNA synthesis led to increased loading of DNA polymerases.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract based on experimental data.

claim: Inhibiting DNA synthesis was accompanied by accumulation of the single-stranded DNA binding protein on the chromatin and activation of DNA helicases.
source: This was accompanied by accumulation of the single-stranded DNA binding protein on the chromatin and activation of DNA helicases further restricting local chromatin motion.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract based on experimental observations.

claim: It is the loading of replisomes but not their catalytic activity that reduces the dynamics of replicating chromatin segments in the S-phase.
source: We, therefore, propose that it is the loading of replisomes but not their catalytic activity that reduces the dynamics of replicating chromatin segments in the S-phase as well as their accessibility and probability of interactions with other genomic regions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: The movement of chromatin loci was shown to be consistent with an anomalous (constrained) diffusion model.
source: The movement of chromatin loci was shown to be consistent with an anomalous (constrained) diffusion model (Scipioni et al., 2018; Shukron et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A single chromatin locus is corralled within a sub-micron radius and exhibits random diffusion motion.
source: This model indicates that a single chromatin locus is corralled within a sub-micron radius and exhibits random diffusion motion and will execute multiple random jumps into neighboring compartments (Bronshtein et al., 2016; Chubb et al., 2002; Heun et al., 2001; Levi et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Some studies have reported that chromatin mobility is enhanced due to active transcription.
source: Some studies have reported that chromatin mobility is enhanced due to active transcription (Gu et al., 2018; Tunnacliffe and Chubb, 2020), whereas others report rather a decrease in mobility (Mach et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from cited studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Other studies report a decrease in chromatin mobility due to active transcription.
source: Some studies have reported that chromatin mobility is enhanced due to active transcription (Gu et al., 2018; Tunnacliffe and Chubb, 2020), whereas others report rather a decrease in mobility (Mach et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from cited studies showing conflicting results.

claim: Chromatin mobility at the sites of double-stranded DNA breaks increases concomitant with their repair.
source: Conversely, there is an established view that chromatin mobility at the sites of double-stranded DNA breaks increases concomitant with their repair (Eaton and Zidovska, 2020; Hauer and Gasser, 2017a; Hauer and Gasser, 2017a; Hauer et al., 2017b; Nagai et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromatin undergoes coherent micron-scale motion at the time scales of 5–10 s independently of the cell cycle stage in mammalian cells.
source: Analysis of fluorescently tagged histones using displacement correlation spectroscopy has shown that chromatin undergoes coherent micron-scale motion at the time scales of 5–10 s independently of the cell cycle stage in mammalian cells (Zidovska et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The correlated motion of chromatin was ATP-dependent and completely disappeared upon DNA damage induction.
source: Furthermore, the correlated motion of chromatin was ATP-dependent and completely disappeared upon DNA damage induction (Eaton and Zidovska, 2020; Zidovska et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual heterologous loci became constrained in S-phase when integrated close to early- and late-firing replication origins in budding yeast.
source: An early study in budding yeast (Heun et al., 2001) demonstrated that individual heterologous loci became constrained in S-phase when integrated close to early- and late-firing replication origins, but not at the telomeric or centromeric regions.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study in yeast.

claim: Changes in chromatin mobility in S-phase were not observed when analyzing it at the level of chromosome territories in mammalian cells.
source: However, changes in chromatin mobility in S-phase were not observed when analyzing it at the level of chromosome territories in mammalian cells (Walter et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Local chromatin motion is restricted upon S-phase entry and more markedly in mid-late S-phase.
source: Recent work using a CRISPR-based DNA imaging system suggests that local chromatin motion is restricted upon S-phase entry and more markedly in mid-late S-phase (Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Cy3-dUTP is incorporated into the nascent DNA of cells in various periods of S-phase, effectively labeling the chromatin directly in an unbiased manner.
source: The nucleotide is incorporated into the nascent DNA of the cells in various periods of S-phase, effectively labeling the chromatin directly in an unbiased manner (Manders et al., 1999; Sadoni et al., 2004; Schermelleh et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement describes the experimental method and is supported by citations.

claim: The Cy3-dUTP-labeled chromatin structures were stable over the cell cycle progression and in subsequent cell cycles.
source: The Cy3-dUTP-labeled chromatin structures were stable over the cell cycle progression and in subsequent cell cycles.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The highest frequency of average DNA amount per focus was about 300–600 kbp of DNA.
source: The highest frequency of average DNA amount per focus (mode +1 bin) was about 300–600 kbp of DNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the DNA quantification analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: With the labeling approach, DNA domains of sizes ranging from 0.5 Mbp to 10 Mbp were labeled, with the vast majority corresponding to 0.5 Mbp.
source: Altogether, with our labeling approach, we labeled DNA domains of sizes ranging from 0.5 Mbp to 10 Mbp, with the vast majority corresponding to 0.5 Mbp, which correspond well to multi-loop chromatin domains corresponding in size to topological associated domains (reviewed in Giorgetti and Heard, 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of the DNA quantification results with a citation to support the interpretation.

claim: Chromatin motion decreases in the S-phase of the cell cycle relative to the G1 and G2 phases.
source: Chromatin motion decreases in the S-phase of the cell cycle relative to the G1 and G2 phases
evidence: This is the title of a results section and a primary finding of the study.

claim: Significantly constrained global chromatin motion was observed in S-phase cells compared to non-replicating G1/G2 cells.
source: We observed significantly constrained global chromatin motion in S-phase cells compared to non-replicating G1/G2 cells suggesting that chromatin was more constrained during DNA replication.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the motion analysis experiments.

claim: The effect of constrained chromatin motion in S-phase was stronger in IMR90 cells compared to HeLa Kyoto.
source: This effect was stronger in IMR90 cells compared to HeLa Kyoto.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the experimental data.

claim: For HeLa, the average diffusion rate of chromatin in G1/G2 was D=133.6 μm2/s × 10–5, whereas the diffusion rates dropped to D=105.6 μm2/s × 10–5 during S-phase.
source: For HeLa average diffusion rate of chromatin in G1/G2 was D=133.6 μm2/s × 10–5, whereas the diffusion rates dropped to D=105.6 μm2/s × 10–5 during S-phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the motion analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For IMR90, the average diffusion rate of chromatin in G1/G2 was D=86.5 μm2/s × 10–5, whereas the diffusion rates dropped to D=43.7 μm2/s × 10–5 during S-phase.
source: For IMR90 average diffusion rate of chromatin in G1/G2 was D=86.5 μm2/s × 10–5, whereas the diffusion rates dropped to D=43.7 μm2/s × 10–5 during S-phase (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the motion analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chromatin exhibited anomalous subdiffusion or obstructed diffusion with 0.1 < ɑ < 0.9.
source: Chromatin exhibited anomalous subdiffusion or obstructed diffusion with 0.1 < ɑ < 0.9.
evidence: This is a characterization of the type of motion observed in the experiments.

claim: Anomalous diffusion of cellular structures including chromatin with α values between 0.1 and 0.9 have been reported.
source: Anomalous diffusion of cellular structures including chromatin with α values between 0.1 and 0.9 have been reported (Bronshtein et al., 2015; Ghosh and Webb, 1994; Mach et al., 2022; Oliveira et al., 2021; Simson et al., 1998; Smith et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromatin in the proximity of replication sites (actively replicating) had more restricted motion when located up to 1 μm (center to center) distance to an active replisome.
source: However, we observed that the chromatin in the proximity of replication sites (actively replicating) had more restricted motion when located up to 1 μm (center to center) distance to an active replisome, and this effect vanished at higher distances (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the proximity analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNA synthesis was inhibited minutes after aphidicolin treatment.
source: We observed that DNA synthesis was inhibited minutes after aphidicolin treatment.
evidence: This is an observation from the EdU incorporation experiments.

claim: In almost 99% of the cell population, DNA replication was inhibited within half an hour of aphidicolin incubation.
source: Using high-content microscopy, we quantified the population of cells actively synthesizing DNA (EdU signal) upon stress and observed that in almost 99% of the cell population, DNA replication was inhibited within half an hour of aphidicolin incubation (Materials and methods, Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the high-throughput imaging analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PCNA dissociated from DNA during aphidicolin treatment.
source: During aphidicolin treatment though, PCNA dissociated from DNA as shown before (Görisch et al., 2008; Rausch et al., 2021; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from live cell imaging supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RPA accumulated over time on DNA at replication sites in aphidicolin-treated cells but not in the control cells.
source: We observed that RPA accumulated over time on DNA at replication sites in aphidicolin-treated cells but not in the control cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no significant changes in MCM2 helicase subunit levels on chromatin upon aphidicolin treatment.
source: We found no significant changes in MCM2 helicase subunit levels on chromatin and higher levels of phosphorylation of MCM2 upon treatment with aphidicolin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Higher levels of phosphorylation of MCM2 were observed upon treatment with aphidicolin.
source: We found no significant changes in MCM2 helicase subunit levels on chromatin and higher levels of phosphorylation of MCM2 upon treatment with aphidicolin (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DNA polymerase α was enriched on chromatin upon stress.
source: The DNA polymerases showed a different behavior as compared to the DNA polymerase clamp protein, with DNA polymerase α being enriched on chromatin upon stress, with only minor to no changes being observed for the processive DNA polymerases δ and ε (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Only minor to no changes were observed for the processive DNA polymerases δ and ε upon aphidicolin treatment.
source: The DNA polymerases showed a different behavior as compared to the DNA polymerase clamp protein, with DNA polymerase α being enriched on chromatin upon stress, with only minor to no changes being observed for the processive DNA polymerases δ and ε (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the western blot and immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: PCNA dissociated from chromatin upon aphidicolin treatment as shown by high-throughput microscopy analysis.
source: We found that PCNA dissociated from chromatin and RPA accumulated on chromatin upon stress in accordance with our previous analysis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the high-throughput microscopy analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RPA accumulated on chromatin upon aphidicolin treatment as shown by high-throughput microscopy analysis.
source: We found that PCNA dissociated from chromatin and RPA accumulated on chromatin upon stress in accordance with our previous analysis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the high-throughput microscopy analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: There were no changes in MCM2 helicase subunit but an increase in active MCM2p108 levels upon stress.
source: We found no changes in MCM2 helicase subunit but an increase in active MCM2p108 levels upon stress.
evidence: This is a finding from the high-throughput microscopy analysis.

claim: The increase in active MCM2p108 is consistent with no new loading of DNA helicases but de novo activation of already loaded helicase complexes.
source: This is consistent with no new loading of DNA helicases but de novo activation of already loaded helicase complexes (Ge et al., 2007; Ibarra et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Significant accumulation of DNA polymerases α and δ on chromatin was observed after aphidicolin treatment.
source: Finally, we observed significant accumulation of DNA polymerases α and δ on chromatin after aphidicolin treatment.
evidence: This is a finding from the high-throughput microscopy analysis.

claim: Chromatin motion was unaffected in G1/G2 cells after aphidicolin treatment.
source: We observed that chromatin motion was unaffected in G1/G2, which fit with our prediction, as in G1/G2 there is no active DNA synthesis besides possible DNA repair processes on a limited genomic scale (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the motion analysis after aphidicolin treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Aphidicolin treatment and inhibition of DNA synthesis led to additional decrease in chromatin motion in S-phase.
source: Surprisingly, aphidicolin treatment and inhibition of DNA synthesis led to additional decrease in chromatin motion (Figure 6B) and the chromatin became even more constrained than at the proximity of the active replication sites in S-phase cells (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the motion analysis after aphidicolin treatment shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The chromatin became even more constrained after aphidicolin treatment than at the proximity of the active replication sites in S-phase cells.
source: Surprisingly, aphidicolin treatment and inhibition of DNA synthesis led to additional decrease in chromatin motion (Figure 6B) and the chromatin became even more constrained than at the proximity of the active replication sites in S-phase cells (see Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the motion analysis.

claim: The accumulation of the helicase and polymerase complexes on chromatin together with the continuous loading of the ssDNA binding protein (RPA) covering the ssDNA strands stiffens the DNA polymer and restricts its diffusional motion.
source: In summary, we propose that the accumulation of the helicase and polymerase complexes on chromatin together with the continuous loading of the ssDNA binding protein (RPA) covering the ssDNA strands stiffens the DNA polymer and restricts its diffusional motion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion proposed by the authors based on their experimental findings.

claim: Aphidicolin is a tetracyclic antibiotic isolated from Nigrospora sphaerica, which interferes with DNA replication directly by inhibiting DNA polymerases α, ε, and δ.
source: Aphidicolin is a tetracyclic antibiotic isolated from Nigrospora sphaerica, which interferes with DNA replication directly by inhibiting DNA polymerases α, ε, and δ (Bambara and Jessee, 1991; Baranovskiy et al., 2014; Byrnes, 1984; Cheng and Kuchta, 1993).
evidence: This is a description of the drug used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: PCNA is a core component of the DNA replication machinery and a marker for cell cycle progression.
source: PCNA is a core component of the DNA replication machinery and a marker for cell cycle progression (Figure 1A; Chagin et al., 2016; Easwaran et al., 2005; Leonhardt et al., 2000; Moldovan et al., 2007; Prelich et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a description of PCNA supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During S-phase, PCNA accumulates within the nucleus at sites of active DNA replication and exhibits a distinct puncta pattern.
source: During S-phase, proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) accumulates within the nucleus at sites of active DNA replication and exhibits a distinct puncta pattern.
evidence: This is a description of PCNA behavior during S-phase shown in Figure 1A.

claim: During G1 and G2, GFP-PCNA is diffusely distributed throughout the nucleus.
source: During G1 and G2, GFP-PCNA is diffusely distributed throughout the nucleus.
evidence: This is a description of PCNA behavior during G1 and G2 shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The genome size of HeLa Kyoto cells is GS = 9.682 ± 0.002 Gbp.
source: The genome size of HeLa Kyoto cells is GS = 9.682 ± 0.002 Gbp (Chagin et al., 2016) and for IMR90 fibroblasts the genome size is 6.37 Gbp as measured earlier (Nichols et al., 1977).
evidence: This is a measurement cited from a previous study.

claim: For IMR90 fibroblasts the genome size is 6.37 Gbp.
source: The genome size of HeLa Kyoto cells is GS = 9.682 ± 0.002 Gbp (Chagin et al., 2016) and for IMR90 fibroblasts the genome size is 6.37 Gbp as measured earlier (Nichols et al., 1977).
evidence: This is a measurement cited from a previous study.

claim: The phosphorylated form of MCM2 is the active form for DNA unwinding.
source: It has been previously described that the phosphorylated form of MCM2 is the active form for DNA unwinding (Forsburg, 2004; Montagnoli et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PCNA does not associate with DNA polymerase α, which has a low processivity.
source: PCNA does not associate with DNA polymerase α, which has a low processivity, but it associates with DNA polymerases ε and δ, which constitute the processive synthetic machinery responsible for most of the duplication of the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA and DNA polymerases.

claim: PCNA associates with DNA polymerases ε and δ, which constitute the processive synthetic machinery responsible for most of the duplication of the genome.
source: PCNA does not associate with DNA polymerase α, which has a low processivity, but it associates with DNA polymerases ε and δ, which constitute the processive synthetic machinery responsible for most of the duplication of the genome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PCNA and DNA polymerases.

claim: The increase in DNA polymerase α could lead to the recruitment of alternative polymerase clamp 9-1-1.
source: The increase in DNA polymerase α could lead to the recruitment of alternative polymerase clamp 9-1-1 as reported before (Michael et al., 2000; Van et al., 2010; Yan and Michael, 2009a; Yan and Michael, 2009b).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The labeled DNA domains correspond well to multi-loop chromatin domains corresponding in size to topological associated domains.
source: Altogether, with our labeling approach, we labeled DNA domains of sizes ranging from 0.5 Mbp to 10 Mbp, with the vast majority corresponding to 0.5 Mbp, which correspond well to multi-loop chromatin domains corresponding in size to topological associated domains (reviewed in Giorgetti and Heard, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DNA quantification results supported by a citation.

claim: Firing of origins of replication by the activation of DNA helicase complexes followed by the loading of synthetic polymerase complexes tracks chromatin compaction.
source: In that sense, firing of origins of replication by the activation of DNA helicase complexes followed by the loading of synthetic polymerase complexes tracks chromatin compaction and upon DNA duplication the focal chromatin organization at multiple hierarchical levels is preserved and can be detected over several cell generations (Cremer et al., 2020; Jackson and Pombo, 1998; Sadoni et al., 2004; Sparvoli et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Upon DNA duplication the focal chromatin organization at multiple hierarchical levels is preserved and can be detected over several cell generations.
source: In that sense, firing of origins of replication by the activation of DNA helicase complexes followed by the loading of synthetic polymerase complexes tracks chromatin compaction and upon DNA duplication the focal chromatin organization at multiple hierarchical levels is preserved and can be detected over several cell generations (Cremer et al., 2020; Jackson and Pombo, 1998; Sadoni et al., 2004; Sparvoli et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genome replication is the only DNA metabolic process that encompasses the entire genome.
source: Importantly, genome replication is the only DNA metabolic process that encompasses the entire genome, thus ensuring the preservation of the genetic material upon cell division.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about genome replication.

claim: The eukaryotic nucleus is a complex subcellular organelle where DNA metabolism, including its replication, repair, and transcription, occurs.
source: The eukaryotic nucleus is a complex subcellular organelle where DNA metabolism, including its replication, repair, and transcription, occurs.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the nucleus.

claim: Eukaryotic DNA is organized in the nuclear space by interactions with histones and architectural proteins to form a hierarchy of domains and compartments of the interphase chromatin.
source: Eukaryotic DNA is organized in the nuclear space by interactions with histones and architectural proteins to form a hierarchy of domains and compartments of the interphase chromatin.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about chromatin organization.

claim: The 4D organization of the chromatin inherently includes its physical properties as a long polymer.
source: According to the current paradigm, the 4D organization of the chromatin inherently includes its physical properties as a long polymer (Esposito et al., 2021; Esposito et al., 2019), while stochastic thermodynamically driven events are likely to play a key role in the domain organization of the chromatin (Conte et al., 2020; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017) and in the regulation of genomic processes (Hnisz et al., 2017; Kilic et al., 2019; Laghmach et al., 2021; Nozaki et al., 2017; Spegg and Altmeyer, 2021; Uchino et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stochastic thermodynamically driven events are likely to play a key role in the domain organization of the chromatin.
source: According to the current paradigm, the 4D organization of the chromatin inherently includes its physical properties as a long polymer (Esposito et al., 2021; Esposito et al., 2019), while stochastic thermodynamically driven events are likely to play a key role in the domain organization of the chromatin (Conte et al., 2020; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017) and in the regulation of genomic processes (Hnisz et al., 2017; Kilic et al., 2019; Laghmach et al., 2021; Nozaki et al., 2017; Spegg and Altmeyer, 2021; Uchino et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stochastic thermodynamically driven events are likely to play a key role in the regulation of genomic processes.
source: According to the current paradigm, the 4D organization of the chromatin inherently includes its physical properties as a long polymer (Esposito et al., 2021; Esposito et al., 2019), while stochastic thermodynamically driven events are likely to play a key role in the domain organization of the chromatin (Conte et al., 2020; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017) and in the regulation of genomic processes (Hnisz et al., 2017; Kilic et al., 2019; Laghmach et al., 2021; Nozaki et al., 2017; Spegg and Altmeyer, 2021; Uchino et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: DNA replication is a highly conserved energy-dependent process occurring in S-phase of the cell cycle.
source: DNA replication is a highly conserved energy-dependent process occurring in S-phase of the cell cycle, when chromatin structures undergo extensive reorganization to facilitate DNA synthesis (Vincent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: During S-phase, chromatin structures undergo extensive reorganization to facilitate DNA synthesis.
source: DNA replication is a highly conserved energy-dependent process occurring in S-phase of the cell cycle, when chromatin structures undergo extensive reorganization to facilitate DNA synthesis (Vincent et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The removal of RNA polymerase II from chromatin relaxes chromatin and increases its mobility.
source: It has been also shown that the removal of RNA polymerase II from chromatin relaxes chromatin and increases its mobility (Babokhov et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The coherent motion of chromatin extended beyond individual chromosomes, suggesting mechanical coupling between chromosomes.
source: This coherent motion extended beyond individual chromosomes, suggesting mechanical coupling between chromosomes.
evidence: This is an interpretation from a cited study about chromatin motion.
